findings.title: Backup code login bypasses password when a totpCode is also supplied
findings.body: The password verification block at line 121 only runs when `credentials.totpCode` is falsy. The new backup-code branch at line 131 is chosen whenever `credentials.backupCode` is present, and it never verifies the password itself. A caller can therefore authenticate with `email`, a valid `backupCode`, and any non-empty `totpCode` (for example `000000`): the truthy `totpCode` skips password verification, then the backup code is validated and authorize returns the user. A stolen/leaked backup code alone becomes sufficient to sign in, defeating two-factor protection.

findings.title: Backup code single-use consumption is not atomic
findings.body: The code reads `user.backupCodes`, validates the submitted code with `indexOf`, and then later writes the whole array back with the matched index set to `null`. There is no transaction or conditional update. Two concurrent requests using the same backup code can both pass validation before either write happens, so both sessions are authorized. Requests using different backup codes can also lose updates because each writes a stale array, leaving an already-used code active. The one-time-code guarantee should be enforced with an atomic/conditional update.

findings.title: First 2FA enable test does not close the new backup-code screen before asserting state
findings.body: `handleEnable` now leaves the modal on the new `DisplayBackupCodes` screen and does not call `onEnable` until the `backup-codes-close` button is clicked. This test enters the OTP and immediately asserts the two-factor switch is checked, so it checks state before the parent is notified/refetched. The second test was updated to click `backup-codes-close` and assert `data-state="checked"`; this test should do the same. As written it either fails or passes due to the already-noted unreliable `isChecked()` assertion.
